list.listitem: Consider a diagnosis of lichen planus (LP) in middle-aged patients who present with bilateral, symmetric, reticular, atrophic, or erosive oral lesions with or without coexisting pruritic, planar, polygonal, purple papules and plaques of the skin. C
Perform a biopsy of mucous membrane or cutaneous lesions to confirm the clinical diagnosis or when dysplasia or malignancy is suspected. C
Consider using topical steroids and topical calcineurin inhibitors to decrease pain in patients with symptomatic oral lichen planus (OLP). B
Consider using oral acitretin, mycophenolate, azathioprine, methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and griseofulvin in the short-term treatment of patients with widespread, symptomatic cutaneous LP. B

background.definition: Lichen planus is a chronic autoimmune, mucocutaneous disorder of unknown etiology. Mucous membrane LP can exist without cutaneous manifestations and frequently involves the oral cavity (ie, oral lichen planus [OLP]). Occasionally, the genital mucous membranes may be affected. Cutaneous LP, which often coexists with OLP, is characterized by pruritic, planar (flat-topped), polygonal, purple papules and plaques (6 P's). Other nonoral forms may involve the scalp, hair, and nails.

list.listitem: Globally, the overall estimated pooled prevalence of oral lichen planus (OLP) is approximately 0.89–1.01% for the general population and 0.98% for clinic-based studies.
Prevalence of OLP varies by geography: from a low of 0.38% in Malaysia to as high as 2.6% in India.
OLP in Japan: males 59.7/100,000 person-years, females 188/100,000 person-years.
LP (unspecified) in UK: males 32/100,000 person-years, females 37/100,000 person-years.
Female to male ratio of OLP = 2 to 3:1. Mean age of onset of LP (unspecified) is 40 years for men and 46 years for women. For oral LP it is 47 years for men and 57 years for women.
OLP is a relatively common condition seen in oral medicine clinics.
Pain is the main presenting symptom.
Autoimmune.

Risk factors include age 30 to 60 years, female sex, and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection (in some countries, eg, Italy and Japan). In a 2023 bidirectional systematic review and meta-analysis, LP (including OLP) showed a significant association with HCV infection (pooled OR ~2.5–5.0 depending on direction and region; stronger in endemic areas and confirmed even in non-Asian populations).

Although LP's etiology is yet to be identified, its immune-mediated pathogenesis is well established. Modified keratinocyte surface antigens elicit a cytotoxic CD8+ cell response that eventually leads to degeneration of the basal cell layer.

Characteristic histologic changes of affected epithelium include: band-like, mainly lymphocytic, immunoinflammatory infiltrates next to the basement membrane, with resulting liquefaction degeneration of the basement membrane and destruction of basal keratinocytes.
Consider cutaneous lichen planus (LP) in middle-aged patients presenting with the 6 P's of pruritic, planar, polygonal, purple papules and plaques of the skin. C
The typical distribution of cutaneous LP is on the wrists, ankles, lower back, eyelids, shins, scalp, penis, or vulva. C
Consider oral lichen planus (OLP) in middle-aged patients who present with bilateral, symmetrical, reticular, atrophic, or erosive oral lesions with or without coexisting skin lesions. C
Biopsy mucous membrane or cutaneous lesions to confirm the clinical diagnosis or when dysplasia or malignancy is suspected. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Clinically difficult to distinguish from OLP except upon identification of causative agents like dental restorative materials (eg, amalgam) in the case of oral lichenoid contact lesions or history of bone marrow transplantation in oral lichenoid lesions of graft-versus-host disease

Clinically difficult to distinguish from cutaneous LP except upon identification of offending drugs (eg, penicillamine, gold, chloroquine, methyldopa), chemical exposure (eg, film processing), or bacterial infections (eg, secondary syphilis)
May be clinically indistinguishable from OLP; do biopsy to establish histologic diagnosis
Tongue almost always involved; white, firmly adherent plaques; responsive to antifungals

Usually confined to vulva, perianal area, and groin; lesions are small, smooth, pink or ivory, flat-topped, slightly raised papules. White-to-brown, horny follicular plugs appear on the surface. Penile, vulvar, or anal lesions appear as white, atrophic plaques
Presence of skin blisters that are preceded by painful oral erosions
Usually appears as desquamative gingivitis; eye involvement very common
Oral lesions along with other cutaneous symptoms (cutaneous LE) or multisystem disease (systemic LE)

list.listitem: Consider cutaneous LP when a patient presents with flat-topped papules on the wrists, ankles, lower back, eyelids, shins, scalp, penis, or vulva. Look for the classic findings of pruritic, planar (flat-topped), polygonal, purple papules and plaques (6 P's) on the skin.
Several cutaneous forms exist: papular, hypertrophic, generalized, follicular, actinic, annular, atrophic, linear, ulcerative, and vesiculobullous.

Consider OLP in patients with bilateral, symmetric lesions that involve the buccal mucosa, dorsum, or lateral borders of the tongue and gingiva. Oral lesions can present as white striations (Wickham's striae), white papules, white plaques, erythema, erosions, or blisters. These oral lesions correspond to 6 clinical forms: reticular, papular, plaque-like, atrophic, erosive, and bullous. More than 1 clinical form may be present at any given time.

See for modified World Health Organization (WHO) diagnostic criteria of OLP. The original WHO diagnostic criteria of 1978, which used histopathologic criteria alone, correlated poorly with the clinical diagnosis of OLP. Thus revised criteria, which combine both clinical and histopathologic features, have been proposed. However, the revised criteria remain to be validated.

Unlike the modified WHO criteria of OLP, there are no established diagnostic criteria for cutaneous LP. The same histopathologic criteria (from the modified WHO diagnostic criteria of OLP) have been used in the literature for cutaneous LP.

A simpler OLP classification system combines the 6 clinical forms discussed above into 3 classes: (1) reticular (reticular, papular, and plaque-like forms); (2) atrophic (erythematous areas of thinned but unbroken epithelium, including the gingival condition desquamative gingivitis); and (3) erosive lesions (epithelium is usually broken; includes bullous form). Reticular lesions are often painless; both atrophic and erosive forms typically cause burning. The reticular and erosive types are the predominant forms at initial presentation.

Vulvar LP (VLP) may be present in up to 57% of women with OLP. Vulvar lesions appear in 3 clinical patterns: papular, erosive/atrophic, and hypertrophic. The majority of patients with VLP are symptomatic (eg, have burning, pruritus, and/or dyspareunia).
Lichen planopilaris is a variant of LP that affects the hair follicles of the scalp causing perifollicular erythema and scale, and may lead to scarring alopecia.

The evidence regarding the diagnostic utility of performing biopsy for histologic confirmation of mucous membrane or cutaneous LP is weak. However, given the chronic and symptomatic nature of mucous membrane LP (ie, OLP and VLP), as well as the need for long-term treatment and monitoring, biopsy may be advisable, especially in clinically atypical cases or when malignancy or dysplasia is suspected.
Studies have shown significant variability in the interobserver and intraobserver reliability in both clinical and histopathologic assessment of OLP based on the original WHO diagnostic criteria.

The modified WHO diagnostic criteria for OLP, while remaining in need of validation, include specific histopathologic criteria that have been useful in standardizing the diagnosis of both mucous membrane and cutaneous LP in clinical trials (see ).

The evidence to support the usefulness of direct immunofluorescence as an adjunct to biopsy of mucous membrane and cutaneous lesions is not definitive. This test is usually employed to rule out specific autoimmune diseases like pemphigus and pemphigoid.
Routine HCV testing of American patients with OLP is not indicated, although it may be appropriate in countries where the association is stronger (eg, Italy, Japan).
Suspect LP in patients with pruritic, planar (flat-topped), polygonal, purple papules and plaques.
See for modified WHO diagnostic criteria for oral lesions.
Consider biopsy to confirm diagnosis.
Consider using topical steroids and topical calcineurin inhibitors, specifically tacrolimus, to decrease pain in patients with symptomatic oral lichen planus (OLP). B
Consider using oral acitretin, mycophenolate, azathioprine, methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and griseofulvin in the short-term treatment of patients with widespread, symptomatic cutaneous LP. B
Current treatments for OLP are not curative; the goal is to relieve pain or discomfort.

A systematic review of 35 RCTs found only weak evidence for the effectiveness of topical steroids and topical calcineurin inhibitors (specifically tacrolimus) for managing pain and clinical symptoms of OLP over the course of treatment (one week to six months). Three studies compared topical corticosteroids with placebo and found low-certainty evidence that steroids may decrease pain more than placebo. Three RCTs compared topical corticosteroids with topical tacrolimus and found very low-certainty evidence that tacrolimus may be better in decreasing pain than steroids. However, the results of the systematic review were inconclusive with regards to clinical response and adverse effects when topical steroids are compared with placebo. Similarly, there is uncertainty regarding the clinical response and adverse events when topical tacrolimus is compared to topical steroids.

A systematic review of 15 RCTs suggested weak evidence from single studies for the effectiveness of topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors (eg, cyclosporin, pimecrolimus), and topical aloe vera for erosive OLP and no evidence for erosive genital LP.

Both every other day intralesional polysaccharide nucleic acid fraction of bacillus Calmette-Guerin or triamcinolone acetonide (10 mg) were found effective in healing erosive OLP at 2 weeks (87.1% vs 88%, respectively). Recurrence rates were similar (33.3% vs 45.5%, respectively).

A small RCT involving 64 patients found the combination of topical triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% plus oral acitretin (25-35 mg/d) was superior to topical triamcinolone monotherapy in adult patients with symptomatic OLP in achieving at least a 75% reduction in disease severity after 28 weeks (88% vs 47%, 95% CI 20-61; P < .001; NNT = 2.4) and after 36 weeks (84% vs 41%, 95% CI 23-67; P < .001; NNT = 2.3).

A systematic review evaluating therapies for cutaneous LP, which included 11 RCTs, found weak evidence that short-term systemic treatment with acitretin, griseofulvin, and sulfasalazine was better than placebo in causing remission or clinical improvement, but cautioned that side-effects were higher in the acitretin and sulfasalazine-treated arms. One RCT showed similar efficacy for oral prednisolone and placebo. Do not use acitretin in women of childbearing potential and monitor it carefully regardless of gender.
Although methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, dapsone, and phototherapy are being used for the treatment of cutaneous LP, no randomized, placebo-controlled trials have been published.

A systematic review (including 3 RCTs and 2 observational studies) indicated the potential role of vitamin D as an adjuvant treatment for oral lichen planus (OLP). Vitamin D when combined with conventional steroid therapy​ showed significant improvement in symptoms.25
Aloe vera, in a systematic review of two small randomized trials, may be comparable to triamcinolone acetonide paste for treating asymptomatic OLP.
A systematic review and meta-analysis of curcuminoids found no significant effect on erythema, lesion size, or pain in OLP compared with controls (updating earlier single RCTs).
Among patients with symptomatic OLP, purslane, a plant high in antioxidants and Omega-3 fatty acids, was more effective than placebo in effecting a partial or complete response (83% vs 17%).

Consider referral of patients with cutaneous LP, OLP, or VLP to specialists (eg, dentist, oral surgeon, ENT, dermatologist, or gynecologist) if uncertainty exists about clinical diagnosis, if symptoms are persistent despite routine treatment, or if dysplasia or malignancy is suspected.
Spontaneous remission of cutaneous LP after 1 year occurs in 68% of cases. B

In contrast, OLP is chronic, rarely undergoes spontaneous remission (only 2.8%-6.5% of cases), has a variable clinical pattern (with unpredictable and frequent exacerbations), and is a potential source of significant morbidity (eg, chronic burning or pain). B

It is controversial whether OLP has the potential for malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma. Although several retrospective studies have shown a small risk (0.8%) of malignant transformation in both atrophic and erosive forms, a more recent, well-designed prospective study found no increase in risk. B
Because of the potential for malignant transformation, periodic follow-up for OLP is recommended. C

Investigators of an Israeli study found aneuploid cells in 16 individuals with OLP (28.1%); one patient subsequently developed squamous cell carcinoma and 10% of the cells examined were aneuploid. They suggest that finding aneuploid cells in brush samples may increase specificity in predicting malignant transformation.
OLP and cutaneous LP in the older adult tend to be more severe.
OLP and cutaneous LP are much less common in children. Lack of clinical suspicion for LP in this age group has led to high rates and long periods of misdiagnosis.

feature.caption: Modified WHO Diagnostic Criteria of Oral Lichen Planus (OLP) and Oral Lichenoid Lesions (OLLs).
feature.feature_body:
Clinical Criteria
Presence of bilateral, more or less symmetric lesions Presence of lace-like network of slightly raised gray-white lines (reticular pattern) Erosive, atrophic, bullous, and plaque-type lesions are only accepted as a subtype in the presence of reticular lesions elsewhere in the oral mucosa In all other lesions that resemble OLP but do not complete the aforementioned criteria, the term "clinically compatible with" should be used
Histopathologic Criteria Presence of a well-defined band-like zone of cellular infiltration that is confined to the superficial part of the connective tissue, consisting mainly of lymphocytes Signs of "liquefaction degeneration" in the basal cell layer Absence of epithelial dysplasia When the histopathologic features are less obvious, the term "histopathologically compatible with" should be used
Applying Criteria to Diagnosis of OLP and OLL OLP: A diagnosis of OLP requires fulfillment of both clinical and histopathologic criteria OLL: The term OLL will be used under the following conditions: (1) clinically typical of OLP but histopathologically only "compatible with" OLP, (2) histopathologically typical of OLP but clinically only "compatible with" OLP, and (3) clinically "compatible with" OLP and histopathologically "compatible with" OLP From van der Meij EH, van der Waal I. Lack of clinicopathologic correlation in the diagnosis of oral lichen planus based on the presently available diagnostic criteria and suggestions for modifications. J Oral Pathol Med 2003;32:507–512.
